summary: This informational memo describes research challenges for Information-Centric Networking (ICN), an approach where uniquely named data, rather than host locations, is the core Internet principle. Data becomes independent of where it is stored or how it travels. The document surveys open problems that researchers would need to address.

plainLanguage.summary: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) organizes communication around named data rather than the location of a host. RFC 7927 surveys the open research problems this approach creates, from checking content to routing requests and managing caches.

questions: what is a named data object
route by name vs lookup by name
what are the main icn research challenges
subtitle: A research survey of the technical challenges in building a network around named data.

tldr.problem: Content distribution and peer-to-peer systems provide access to named data in overlays, but the underlying network does not see those requests. This can create indirect paths, repeated transfers, and difficulty validating cached content.
tldr.mechanism: Information-Centric Networking treats named data objects as a network service, allowing nodes to forward requests, cache objects, and validate name-content bindings. The RFC surveys research challenges in naming, security, routing, mobility, wireless networks, transport, caching, and management.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7927 is an IRTF research agenda, not a standard. It describes technical challenges and approaches rather than defining an ICN protocol.

today: RFC 7927 is an Informational IRTF research-group document published in July 2016. It states that it does not constitute a standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Consider Information-Centric Networking
sections.content:
Content distribution networks and peer-to-peer applications already provide access to named data objects, but they operate as overlays. Since the network does not see their data requests, traffic may follow paths chosen by the overlay, multicast may be underused, and applications may duplicate caching and authenticity functions.

ICN makes named data objects a first-class network service. Data can be independent of its location, storage, application, and transport, which may enable in-network caching, replication, multicast, and local retransmission. The RFC describes challenges to achieving these benefits, not a finished design.
sections.plainLanguage: Today's network forwards packets between hosts, while applications build their own systems for finding and caching data. ICN would make requests for named data visible to the network itself.

sections.title: Named Objects and Receiver-Driven Requests
sections.content:
A Named Data Object (NDO) is an addressable unit of data with a name bound to it, usually with a way to validate that binding. A requestor asks for an NDO; a publisher makes it available but need not be its creator. ICN names identify data rather than a network node or interface.

Nodes can forward requests and cache objects. If a response's content can be validated against its name, a node can serve a cached copy without proving its own identity. Retrieval is typically receiver-driven: the requestor controls the sending rate by controlling how quickly it sends requests, and it can resend a request after a timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: An ICN request names the data it wants, rather than naming the machine that stores it. A network node can return a cached copy if the data matches its name.

sections.title: Naming, Integrity, and Security
sections.content:
ICN needs unique names and a verifiable binding between each name and its data, because a copy may come from a cache rather than the original source. Hierarchical names can support route aggregation and may be human-readable. Flat hash-based names can bind a content hash or publisher key to an object, but are typically not human-readable and may be harder to aggregate.

Other challenges include naming dynamic objects before they exist, protecting requestor privacy when networks can observe requests, handling updates without changing an existing name-content binding, and limiting access to restricted objects. Security challenges include distributing publisher keys, binding content to real-world identities, access control, encryption, request aggregation and filtering, router state exhaustion, replicated content, and growth of routing tables.
sections.plainLanguage: Because caches can answer requests, a receiver needs a way to verify that returned data matches the requested name. ICN also needs workable ways to keep requests private, manage updates, and restrict access.

sections.title: Routing, Mobility, and Wireless Networks
sections.content:
The RFC describes three routing approaches. Route-By-Name Routing (RBNR) routes directly on a data name, avoiding a resolution step but potentially growing routing tables with the number of objects. Lookup-By-Name Routing (LBNR) first maps a name to a locator and needs fast lookup and update. Hybrid Routing combines the approaches, such as using RBNR within a domain and LBNR between domains.

Mobility is a central ICN research topic, but the RFC says no general solution using native ICN mechanisms had emerged. Wireless networks also create an opportunity: the same data may cross the wireless medium separately for each recipient, even if the access point caches it. The RFC asks how ICN could use the broadcast nature of wireless more effectively.
sections.plainLanguage: ICN can route directly by a data name, look up a location first, or combine both methods. Researchers still need to determine how these designs should handle moving devices and shared wireless transmissions.

sections.title: Transport, Caching, and Management
sections.content:
Receiver-driven requests let a client control its request rate and choose among sources, but caches can create short-lived sub-flows and out-of-order delivery. Round-trip-time measurements may become misleading, and request aggregation makes fairness difficult because a router may not know how many requestors are behind one request.

In-network caching raises questions about where caches belong, which content to store, how requests find a copy, how to detect stale objects, and whether applications can share caches without cache poisoning. ICN also needs management tools suited to named data rather than only nodes and end-to-end packet streams.

The RFC notes that web applications need to map request context, video could use caching and multiple sources, and IoT applications often need publisher-initiated updates even though ICN is receiver-driven.
sections.plainLanguage: Caches can make data closer to users, but they complicate rate measurement, fairness, and finding fresh copies. Management tools and applications also need ways to work with named objects.
